section.title: We Have Sinned Like Our Fathers
section.sectionRationale: The closing psalm of Book IV, Psalms 90 to 106, and the deliberate companion of Psalm 105: where that psalm rehearsed God's covenant faithfulness, this one confesses Israel's repeated rebellion across the very same history, from the Red Sea to the wilderness to the land of Canaan. It ends with a doxology that closes the whole book, and with a plea to be gathered from among the nations, a prayer answered in part at the return from exile and finally in Christ's gathering of His scattered people.
section.thesis: Israel's history, from the Red Sea through the golden calf, the refusal of the promised land, Baal of Peor, and generations of idolatry in Canaan, is one long record of forgetting God's works, yet at every turn His steadfast love, not Israel's worthiness, is what saves, relents, and finally gathers His people home.
section.frameNote: Eight movements: a call to praise and a personal plea, verses 1 to 5; rebellion and rescue at the Red Sea, verses 6 to 12; craving and envy in the wilderness, verses 13 to 18; the golden calf and Moses' intercession, verses 19 to 23; refusing the promised land, verses 24 to 27; Baal of Peor and the zeal of Phinehas, verses 28 to 31; Meribah and the failure to drive out the nations, verses 32 to 39; and judgment, mercy, and a closing plea to gather Israel from the nations, verses 40 to 48.

units.label: Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good
units.note: a call to praise and a personal plea

verses.text: Hallelujah! Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His {{chesed|loving devotion}} endures forever.
Who can describe the mighty acts of the LORD or fully proclaim His praise?
Blessed are those who uphold justice, who practice righteousness at all times.
Remember me, O LORD, in Your favor to Your people; visit me with Your salvation,
that I may see the prosperity of Your chosen ones, and rejoice in the gladness of Your nation, and give glory with Your inheritance.

units.label: We have sinned like our fathers
units.note: rebellion and rescue at the Red Sea

verses.text: We have sinned like our fathers; we have done wrong and acted wickedly.
Our fathers in Egypt did not grasp Your wonders or remember Your abundant kindness; but they rebelled by the sea, there at the Red Sea.
Yet He saved them for the sake of His name, to make His power known.
He rebuked the Red Sea, and it dried up; He led them through the depths as through a desert.
He saved them from the hand that hated them; He redeemed them from the hand of the enemy.
The waters covered their foes; not one of them remained.
Then they believed His promises and sang His praise.

units.label: They soon forgot His works
units.note: craving and envy in the wilderness

verses.text: Yet they soon forgot His works and failed to wait for His counsel.
They craved intensely in the wilderness and tested God in the desert.
So He granted their request, but sent a wasting disease upon them.
In the camp they envied Moses, as well as Aaron, the holy one of the LORD.
The earth opened up and swallowed Dathan; it covered the assembly of Abiram.
Then fire blazed through their company; flames consumed the wicked.

units.label: They exchanged their Glory
units.note: the golden calf and Moses' intercession

verses.text: At Horeb they made a calf and worshiped a molten image.
They exchanged their Glory for the image of a grass-eating ox.
They forgot God their Savior, who did great things in Egypt,
wondrous works in the land of Ham, and awesome deeds by the Red Sea.
So He said He would destroy them, had not Moses His chosen one stood before Him in the {{peretz|breach}} to divert His wrath from destroying them.
They despised the pleasant land; they did not believe His promise.
They grumbled in their tents and did not listen to the voice of the LORD.
So He raised His hand and swore to cast them down in the wilderness,
to disperse their offspring among the nations and scatter them throughout the lands.

units.label: Phinehas stood and intervened
units.note: Baal of Peor and the zeal of Phinehas

verses.text: They yoked themselves to Baal of Peor and ate sacrifices offered to lifeless gods.
So they provoked the LORD to anger with their deeds, and a plague broke out among them.
But Phinehas stood and intervened, and the plague was restrained.
It was {{chashab|credited}} to him as righteousness for endless generations to come.

units.label: They mingled with the nations
units.note: Meribah and the failure to drive out the nations

verses.text: At the waters of Meribah they angered the LORD, and trouble came to Moses because of them.
For they rebelled against His Spirit, and Moses spoke rashly with his lips.
They did not destroy the peoples as the LORD had commanded them,
but they mingled with the nations and adopted their customs.
They worshiped their idols, which became a snare to them.
They sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons.
They shed innocent blood, the blood of their sons and daughters, whom they sacrificed to the idols of Canaan, and the land was polluted with blood.
They defiled themselves by their actions and prostituted themselves by their deeds.

units.label: Save us, O LORD our God
units.note: judgment, mercy, and a closing plea to gather Israel

verses.text: So the anger of the LORD burned against His people, and He abhorred His own inheritance.
He delivered them into the hand of the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them.
Their enemies oppressed them and subdued them under their hand.
Many times He rescued them, but they were bent on rebellion and sank down in their iniquity.
Nevertheless He heard their cry; He took note of their distress.
And He remembered His covenant with them, and relented by the abundance of His loving devotion.
He made them objects of compassion to all who held them captive.
Save us, O LORD our God, and gather us from the nations, that we may give thanks to Your holy name, that we may glory in Your praise.
Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting. Let all the people say, "Amen!" Hallelujah!

chesed.gloss: Loving devotion, steadfast love, loyal covenant kindness. This word frames the whole psalm, verses 1 and 45, the one constant across a story otherwise marked by human failure.

peretz.gloss: A breach, a gap in a wall or defense. Moses stood in this gap between God's wrath and the people, verse 23, a picture of intercession that the New Testament applies to Christ's own mediating work.

chashab.gloss: To credit, reckon, or count as. The same verb used of Abraham's faith being credited as righteousness, Genesis 15:6; here Phinehas' zealous act is credited to him in the same way, tying this psalm's language directly to the doctrine of righteousness reckoned by grace.

basic.context: This psalm closes Book IV of the Psalter with a national confession: we have sinned like our fathers. It retells the same history as Psalm 105, the Red Sea, the wilderness, the golden calf, Canaan, but from the opposite angle, cataloging Israel's repeated rebellion against a God who kept saving them anyway.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm is corporate confession set inside praise, opening and closing with Hallelujah even though the middle is almost entirely a record of failure. It is meant to be prayed by later generations as their own confession, we have sinned like our fathers, not merely read as ancient history.
basic.originalLanguages: The psalm is bracketed by chesed, God's loving devotion, verses 1 and 45, the one constant thread. Moses stood in the peretz, the breach, verse 23, between God's wrath and the people. Phinehas' zeal was chashab, credited, to him as righteousness, verse 31, the same verb used of Abraham's faith in Genesis 15:6.
basic.typology: Moses standing in the breach to turn away God's wrath, verse 23, prefigures Christ, the greater Mediator who always lives to intercede, Hebrews 7:25. Phinehas' zeal, credited to him as righteousness, verse 31, echoes the pattern of righteousness reckoned by grace that culminates in the gospel, Romans 4:3-5.
basic.christ: Moses' intercession in the breach, verse 23, anticipates Christ, our great High Priest who does not merely delay God's wrath for a moment but bears it fully and lives forever to intercede for His people, Hebrews 7:25, 1 Timothy 2:5. The psalm's closing plea to be gathered from the nations, verse 47, is answered ultimately in Christ's gathering of His scattered sheep into one flock, John 11:52.
basic.god: God is shown as righteously angered by persistent unbelief and idolatry, yet His anger never has the last word; verse after verse of failure is met by rescue, and the psalm's own refrain insists it is for His name's sake and because of His steadfast love, not Israel's merit, that He acts.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 32 records the golden calf in full. Numbers 25 records Baal of Peor and Phinehas' zeal. Hebrews 7:25 presents Christ as the Mediator who always lives to intercede, fulfilling what Moses pictured only partially. Romans 4:3-5 explains righteousness credited by faith, the same word used of Phinehas here.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's long record of Israel forgetting God's works, met again and again by His steadfast love rather than by what they deserved, is the very shape of the gospel, and it finds its resolution in Christ, the Mediator who stands in the ultimate breach and the Shepherd who gathers God's scattered people home for good.

context.literary:
The psalm is built as a long confession with praise on both ends. Hallelujah opens verse 1 and closes verse 48, and between them the speaker moves from a general blessing on the just, verse 3, to a personal plea, verses 4 to 5, and then to the confession proper, which begins with the flat plural of verse 6, 'We have sinned like our fathers.' The words 'sinned', 'done wrong' and 'acted wickedly' are stacked three deep, so the history that follows is not offered as someone else's story. It is a case being laid before God by people who admit they stand in the same line.

The recital runs in rough order of the Pentateuch, but it is selective in a telling way. Egypt, the Red Sea, Kibroth-hattaavah, Dathan and Abiram, the calf at Horeb, the refusal at Kadesh, Baal of Peor and Meribah each get a verse or two, and then the pace changes. Verses 34 to 39 cover the whole Canaan period in a rush, and verses 40 to 46 compress the cycle of the judges and the exile into a single movement of anger, oppression, cry and compassion. The reader is meant to feel the pattern repeating, not to memorise a list.

Two moments of rescue stand out inside the sins. Moses stands in the breach, verse 23, and Phinehas stands and intervenes, verse 30. The same verb of standing is used of both men, and in each case wrath is turned aside by one person who steps between God and the people. Around those two figures the psalm is mostly about people who did not stand, who sank down, verse 43, and sat in their tents grumbling, verse 25.

The ending turns on the one line of petition, verse 47, which the psalm has been preparing all along. A people who have just been described as scattered ask to be gathered, and the doxology that follows is not an afterthought. It is how the psalm insists that confession has not cancelled praise.
context.historical:
The psalm looks back over about a thousand years of national memory, from the Exodus to a period when Israel lived among foreign rulers. Verses 41 to 46 speak of being handed over to the nations and of being given compassion in the eyes of captors. That language fits the experience of the Babylonian exile, and it recalls the prayer Solomon had asked for at the dedication of the temple, that God would grant His people compassion before those who held them captive, 1 Kings 8:50. The closing petition, 'gather us from the nations,' sounds like a people who have not yet fully returned.

Scholars do not agree on a date. Verses 1, 47 and 48 appear in the song David is said to have appointed when the ark was brought to Jerusalem, 1 Chronicles 16:34 to 36, which shows the psalm was known to the Chronicler. Some therefore place it before the exile and read verses 40 to 47 as anticipating judgment; others take it as written from within the exile and later quoted. Either way the setting is a worshipping community that has absorbed the lessons of the prophets.

The sins it names were the ones the prophets and the law had warned against. Baal of Peor was the Moabite cult at Shittim, Numbers 25:1 to 3. The sacrifice of children, verses 37 and 38, is condemned in Deuteronomy 12:31 and is recorded of kings such as Ahaz and Manasseh, 2 Kings 16:3 and 21:6. The psalm's insistence that such blood 'polluted' the land echoes the law's teaching that spilled blood defiles the ground and must be dealt with, Numbers 35:33.

The same long retelling appears in other prayers of confession from the period, notably Nehemiah 9 and the speech of Stephen in Acts 7. Israel clearly had a habit of reciting its own failures in worship, and this psalm is the poetic form of that habit.
context.canonical:
Psalm 106 closes Book IV, which began with the prayer of Moses in Psalm 90. That frame matters. The book that opens with Moses asking God to 'relent' ends with a psalm in which Moses stands in the breach and God does relent, verse 45. Moses is named in Psalms 90, 99, 103, 105 and 106, and the book can be read as Israel learning to live under the LORD's kingship after the loss of the monarchy.

The psalm is the dark twin of Psalm 105. Both retell the Exodus and wilderness, both begin with a call to thanks and both end with Hallelujah. But Psalm 105 tells the story as the faithfulness of the God of Abraham, leaving out Israel's failures almost entirely, while Psalm 106 supplies exactly what 105 left out. Read together they give the two halves of one truth: God keeps covenant, and the people do not.

The wider canon returns to the same material. Ezekiel 20 rehearses Israel's rebellion from Egypt onward and says God acted 'for the sake of My name,' Ezekiel 20:9, the same motive as verse 8 here. Jeremiah 2:11 uses the language of exchanging 'their Glory' that appears in verse 20. In the New Testament Stephen retells the calf, the wilderness and the exile in Acts 7, and Paul warns the Corinthians from the same events, craving, idolatry, immorality, testing and grumbling, in 1 Corinthians 10:6 to 10. Paul says these things 'took place as examples,' which is exactly how the psalmist wanted his own generation to hear them.

The doxology of verse 48 closes the book as the earlier books were closed, Psalm 41:13, 72:18 to 19 and 89:52, and the people's 'Amen' is answered in the first line of Psalm 107.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wants his hearers to refuse the comfortable idea that their ancestors were the problem and they are the cure. By starting with 'We have sinned like our fathers' and only then walking through the history, he makes confession the lens through which the whole past is read. The reader is not allowed to stand outside the story as a judge. The scenes of grumbling, calf worship and compromise are offered as a mirror, and the pronouns slide from 'our fathers' to 'they' to 'we' to show that the line has not broken.

He also wants them to read the history as a record of God's patience, not only of Israel's failure. Each sin is followed by something God does, rescues for His name's sake, grants and then judges, hears a cry, remembers a covenant. By the end the surprise of the poem is not that Israel failed, which every hearer already knew, but that God went on remembering. The petition of verse 47 is therefore not a bargain. It is the request of people who have read their own record and have nothing to plead except what God has already shown about Himself.

Finally, he wants confession to end in worship. The psalm will not let sorrow have the last word, and a congregation praying it was meant to find that it could say 'Hallelujah' honestly because it had first said 'we have sinned.'
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes a catalogue of national failures and the judgments that followed them. It does not command the events, and it does not teach that every disaster in a believer's life is a punishment for a particular sin. The psalm itself is careful here. The wasting disease of verse 15 and the plague of verse 29 are tied to named acts, and the psalm does not generalise from them to every illness.

What it prescribes is a posture. Believers are meant to confess sins in the first person plural, to recite God's past mercies even when they have been faithless, and to ask for rescue on the ground of God's covenant love, not on their own record. Verses 4 and 5 show that personal petition fits inside corporate prayer, and verse 47 shows that hope for restoration is part of the prayer, not a replacement for it.

The harder verses need care. The deaths of Dathan and Abiram and the plague at Peor are narrated, not offered as a model for how any community should deal with offenders today. And Phinehas' violent act is recounted as a unique moment under the covenant of the wilderness; the psalm commends his zeal for God, not his weapon, and the New Testament does not carry it over into the church's practice.

debates.question: Whose Spirit did Israel rebel against at Meribah, verse 33?

views.label: God's own Spirit
views.case: The BSB reads 'they rebelled against His Spirit,' and Isaiah 63:10 says Israel 'rebelled and grieved His Holy Spirit' in the same wilderness setting. On this reading the psalm names the Spirit of God as the one wronged, and Moses 'spoke rashly' because the people had pushed him there. Many Christian interpreters see in this an early glimpse of the personal Spirit whom the New Testament warns believers not to grieve, Ephesians 4:30.

views.label: Moses' spirit
views.case: The BSB footnote offers 'they provoked His Spirit,' and the pronoun could refer back to Moses, who is the nearest person in the verse and who 'spoke rashly with his lips' in the next clause. On this view the people embittered Moses' spirit until he spoke without thought, as Numbers 20:10 records, and the verse is about the human cost of leading a rebellious people.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree that the people's rebellion was real and that it cost Moses dearly. The first gives the verse more doctrinal weight, the second fits the flow of the Hebrew sentence more closely. The safest conclusion is that the psalm links the people's provocation to God's own Spirit as the one who was with Moses, and that Moses' failure is stated plainly because even the greatest intercessor was only a man.

debates.question: What does it mean that Phinehas' act was 'credited to him as righteousness,' verse 31?

views.label: A reward for a righteous deed under the covenant of the wilderness
views.case: Numbers 25:11 to 13 explains that Phinehas turned God's wrath aside and was given a 'covenant of peace' and a permanent priesthood. The psalm summarises this as God counting his act as righteousness, a public verdict that he had done what the covenant required.

views.label: The same grace as Abraham's, seen at work in an act of faith
views.case: The wording is very close to Genesis 15:6, where Abraham's belief is credited as righteousness. Paul uses that verse to show that righteousness is received by faith and not earned, Romans 4:3 to 5. On this view Phinehas' zeal was the fruit of trusting God's covenant, and what was credited was not a wage but a gift.

views.label: A distinct use of the phrase
views.case: Some stress that the context is a deed that preserved a community, not a sinner's standing before God, and warn against reading Romans 4 back into the verse.

debates.bearing: The psalm itself sets this verdict in a poem whose whole argument is that no generation can plead its own record, so it is hard to read verse 31 as a boast. The safest course is to see a real, public commendation of Phinehas that the New Testament later shows to rest on the same free grace that justifies sinners, without claiming that Psalm 106 itself teaches justification by faith.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word of the confession is the most important. 'We have sinned' in verse 6 uses chata, the common word for missing a mark, and it is joined by two other verbs, 'done wrong' and 'acted wickedly.' The three together cover failure of aim, twisting of what is right and active evil. The same threefold confession appears in Solomon's prayer, 1 Kings 8:47, and in Daniel 9:5, which shows the psalm is drawing on a settled liturgical form for national repentance. That form also appears in the law, where Leviticus 26:40 promises that confession of the fathers' sin will open the way to restoration.

In verse 7 the fathers 'did not grasp' God's wonders. The Hebrew verb is sakal, to act with insight or understanding, a root of the wisdom tradition, Proverbs 21:16 is one example. The failure is not forgetfulness only but a refusal to draw conclusions. They saw the plagues and still did not think. The next clause says they did not 'remember' his abundant kindness, using the root zakar, which in Hebrew means to act on what is called to mind. The parallel with verse 4, where the psalmist asks that God would 'remember' him, is deliberate: the people who would not remember God's kindness must now ask to be remembered.

The most striking word is in verse 20. The English 'They exchanged their Glory' translates a form of kavod, the word for weight or glory that Israel used of God's own presence. The footnote notes the alternative 'their glorious God.' Jeremiah 2:11 uses almost the same idiom, 'My people have exchanged their Glory for useless idols,' and Paul draws on it in Romans 1:23 when he writes that the nations 'exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images.' The point is that Israel swapped the living God for something that eats grass. The phrase 'grass-eating ox' mocks the image with a single descriptive word.

In verse 37 the idols of Canaan are called 'demons,' from shedim. The word appears in the Hebrew Bible only here and in Deuteronomy 32:17, where Moses says Israel 'sacrificed to demons, not to God.' The psalm thus places child sacrifice in a spiritual frame: behind the idols stood powers that were not God. Verse 28 uses a similar idea when it says Israel ate sacrifices offered to the 'lifeless' gods, literally the dead.

Verse 23 pictures Moses standing in the breach, peretz. The image is of a broken wall in a city under attack, where a defender must stand in the gap. Ezekiel 22:30 uses the same picture when God says He looked for a man to 'stand in the gap' and found no one. The word thus carries the sense of a defender who takes the full weight of the assault on himself.

Finally, verse 45 says God 'relented,' from nacham, which the same verb in Exodus 32:14 describes of God after Moses' plea. The verb has a range from 'be sorry' to 'comfort' to 'change course.' It does not suggest that God was unsure but that His response is a real response to prayer. Hebrew grammar pairs it here with 'according to the abundance of His chesed,' showing that the ground of relenting is not Moses' eloquence but God's own covenant love.

typology.type: Moses standing in the breach, verse 23
typology.fulfillment: Moses placed himself between a holy God and a guilty people, and wrath was turned away, as the account in Exodus 32:11 to 14 records. Christ is the greater Mediator, 'the one mediator between God and men,' 1 Timothy 2:5, and 'He always lives to intercede,' Hebrews 7:25. The escalation is that Moses could only plead; he could not bear the wrath. Moses even offered his own life, Exodus 32:32, and was refused. Christ was 'made sin' and bore the curse, 2 Corinthians 5:21 and Galatians 3:13, so that the breach was filled by a sacrifice and not merely a request. The type falls short because Moses was himself a sinner who later spoke rashly at Meribah, verse 33.

typology.type: Phinehas' zeal and the covenant of peace, verses 30 and 31
typology.fulfillment: Phinehas stepped into a crisis, ended a plague and received a 'covenant of peace' with a permanent priesthood, Numbers 25:12 and 13. The pattern of a priest whose act turns away wrath and secures a lasting priesthood finds its fulfilment in Christ, a priest 'forever,' Hebrews 7:24 and 25, who made atonement once, Hebrews 9:26. The difference is stark. Phinehas ended a plague by a spear; Christ ended wrath by giving Himself. Phinehas' priesthood continued through descendants who die; Christ's priesthood is held by one who lives forever.

typology.type: The scattering and the gathering, verses 27 and 47
typology.fulfillment: Israel's exile is the shape of the human condition as Scripture sees it, a people scattered from God's presence. The prayer 'gather us from the nations' is answered in part by the return from Babylon, Ezra 1, and finally in Christ, who 'was to die for the nation, and not only for the nation, but also to gather into one the scattered children of God,' John 11:51 and 52. The new people He gathers come from every tribe and language, Revelation 7:9, so the type expands from a nation to the world. It falls short because the first return left Israel still under foreign rule, Nehemiah 9:36.

typology.type: Wilderness failures as warnings for the church, verses 14 to 33
typology.fulfillment: Paul reads the craving, idolatry, immorality, testing and grumbling of the wilderness generation as 'examples,' 1 Corinthians 10:6 to 11, and links the rock at Meribah to Christ, 1 Corinthians 10:4. The correspondence is that every generation of God's people is tempted in the same ways. The escalation is that believers have a greater deliverance and so a greater accountability, Hebrews 3:12 and 13. The type falls short only in that the church has the indwelling Spirit and the finished work of Christ, which the wilderness generation did not yet possess.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ most clearly by the figure of the mediator. In verse 23 God is ready to destroy, and Moses 'His chosen one' stands in the breach. The psalm calls Moses 'chosen,' and that title is later given to the servant of Isaiah 42:1 and, in the Gospels, to Jesus at the transfiguration, Luke 9:35. The scene sets up a question the Old Testament cannot answer by itself: what happens when the one who stands in the breach is himself unworthy? Moses is rebuked at Meribah, verse 33, and is kept out of the land, Numbers 20:12. The psalm quietly shows that the intercessor is not enough.

Christ answers that question. He is 'a great high priest who has passed through the heavens,' Hebrews 4:14, who 'always lives to intercede for those who draw near to God through Him,' Hebrews 7:25. Where Moses stood in a breach in a wall, Christ stood in the breach between God and sinners and took the blow himself, 'bearing our sins in His body on the tree,' 1 Peter 2:24. The psalm's picture of wrath turned away by a man who stood in the gap becomes in the gospel a wrath turned away because a man was struck in the gap. Paul says it plainly: God presented Christ as a propitiation, Romans 3:25, so that He might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus.

The phrase 'credited as righteousness' in verse 31 points to Christ by another road. Phinehas was commended for a deed; believers are credited with a righteousness that is not their own. Paul quotes the verb from Genesis 15:6 to show that the righteousness is credited to those who believe in the One who raised Jesus from the dead, Romans 4:23 to 25. The psalm cannot carry the full weight of that doctrine, but it shows that Scripture already knew a righteousness counted to a person by God's verdict.

The closing prayer, 'gather us from the nations,' also points forward. Caiaphas unknowingly prophesied that Jesus would die 'to gather into one the scattered children of God,' John 11:52. The Good Shepherd who has 'other sheep' to bring in, John 10:16, answers verse 47 on a scale the psalmist could not have imagined, for the gathering includes Gentiles. And the psalm's last word, 'Amen,' is the word Christ uses of Himself, 'the Amen, the faithful and true Witness,' Revelation 3:14, the One in whom every promise of God is 'Yes,' 2 Corinthians 1:20.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The psalm does not predict Jesus by name, and Phinehas' spear is not a picture of the cross. The links rest on the New Testament's own handling of Moses' intercession, of credited righteousness, and of the gathering of the scattered.
study.god:
This psalm shows God first as the one who acts 'for the sake of His name,' verse 8. At the Red Sea Israel had given Him no reason to save them. They had just cried that it would have been better to stay in Egypt, Exodus 14:11 and 12. He saved them anyway, 'to make His power known.' This is not self-regard in a petty sense. It means that God's saving is rooted in who He is, so that the rescue is dependable even when the people are not. The psalm shows the same logic at the end, where relenting rests on His covenant and 'the abundance of His loving devotion,' verse 45.

He is a God who judges sin seriously and specifically. The psalm does not hide the disease that followed craving, the earth that opened, the fire, the plague, the oath to cast them down, or the exile. These are not random disasters; each follows a particular act, and Scripture treats the judgment as just. The psalm also shows that God judges idolatry harshly because it destroys people, not only because it dishonours Him. The children sacrificed to idols were 'innocent blood,' verse 38, and the land itself was polluted. God's anger is the anger of One who loves the people and hates what is killing them.

Yet His anger is never the last word. The same psalm that says He 'abhorred His own inheritance,' verse 40, says He 'took note of their distress,' verse 44, and 'remembered His covenant,' verse 45. The verbs are carefully chosen. To 'remember' in Scripture is to act on a promise, as when God remembered Noah, Genesis 8:1, and Abraham, Genesis 19:29. So the psalm teaches that the covenant is the fixed point and that the shifts in God's dealings with Israel, from anger to compassion, are responses within a faithfulness that does not change. This is the pattern Exodus 34:6 and 7 had announced after the calf: slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion, yet not leaving the guilty unpunished.

He is also a God who listens to prayer, including the prayer of a mediator. The psalm is clear that Moses' standing in the breach mattered, verse 23. This does not mean God is persuaded to be kinder than He wanted to be. It means that the God who is in control of history has also chosen to work through intercession, which gives prayer real weight without diminishing His sovereignty.

For worship, the psalm teaches that praise and confession belong together. A congregation that can say 'we have sinned like our fathers' can also say 'Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting.' The two are not in tension, because the God who is praised is the one who forgives. The psalm also shows that the proper response to His patience is not complacency but the urgent plea of verse 47, 'Save us, O LORD our God.'

crossReferences.note: The Chronicler quotes verses 1, 47 and 48 in the song appointed for the ark's arrival in Jerusalem. It shows that these verses were treated as a unit of worship, and that the plea to be gathered from the nations was already part of Israel's liturgy, ending in the people's 'Amen' and 'Praise the LORD.'

The law's own promise behind the psalm. If the people confess their iniquity and that of their fathers, God says He will remember His covenant. Verse 6 of the psalm is exactly this confession, and verse 45 is exactly this remembering, so the psalm is the law's remedy being prayed.

Moses pleads with God over the calf, and the LORD relents from the disaster He had spoken. This is the scene behind verses 19 to 23, and the same verb for relenting is used in verse 45 to describe God's later dealing with the whole nation.
The account of Phinehas' action at Peor and God's covenant of peace with him. It fills out verses 28 to 31 and shows why the act is remembered as zeal for God, not only as violence.

God looks for a man to stand in the gap and finds none. This is the other side of verse 23. Moses was the one who did stand in the breach, and the contrast shows how rare and precious such an intercessor is.

Jeremiah accuses Israel of exchanging their Glory for useless idols, wording very close to verse 20. It shows that the psalmist and the prophet read Israel's idolatry as the same act: swapping the true God for something that cannot help.

Another prayer of confession that retells the cycle of rebellion, oppression, cry and rescue, with 'many times' of deliverance. It parallels verses 40 to 45 and shows that the same story was prayed in the post-exilic community.

Stephen tells how the fathers refused to obey Moses, turned in their hearts to Egypt and made the calf. He draws the same conclusion as the psalm, that the nation has always resisted God, and it shows that the New Testament reads the psalm's history as a warning.

Paul lists craving, idolatry, immorality, testing and grumbling, each tied to wilderness events that Psalm 106 recounts. He says these things were written 'as examples,' so the psalm functions as a mirror for the church.

Paul explains that credited righteousness belongs to the one who trusts God who justifies the ungodly. The verb used of Phinehas in verse 31 is the one used for Abraham, so the verse is a pointer toward the doctrine Paul develops.

Christ holds His priesthood permanently because He lives forever, and He is able to save completely those who draw near through Him. This is the full answer to the question raised by Moses and Phinehas, whose interventions were real but limited.
John explains that Jesus would die to gather into one the scattered children of God. It is the answer, on a wider scale than the psalmist knew, to the prayer of verse 47.

study.oneStory:
The psalm sits at the point in the Bible's story where a question has become unavoidable: if God rescued Israel, why is Israel scattered? Genesis had already answered the question in miniature. The pair in the garden were driven out because they listened to a rival voice, Genesis 3, and at Babel the nations were scattered, Genesis 11:8. Psalm 106 shows Israel following the same road. They are redeemed from Egypt and brought to the edge of the land, and yet they reproduce the pattern of the garden: they distrust the word, take what is forbidden, and find themselves cast out. The psalm is therefore not just a chapter in Israel's history but a window on the human story, where even the redeemed need a further redemption.

What the psalm sets up is the need for a different kind of mediator and a deeper kind of gathering. Moses stands in the breach and Phinehas intervenes, but neither can change the heart of the people, and both are eventually remembered with a note of sorrow. The Prophets later promise that God Himself will gather His people and give them a new heart, Ezekiel 36:24 to 27, and that He will place His Spirit within them. Those promises are what the closing petition is waiting for.

In Christ, the pattern is reversed at last. The people who are scattered, Jew and Gentile alike, are gathered into one, John 11:52, and the covenant that God remembers is the new covenant in His blood, Luke 22:20. The God who relented for the sake of His name now acts in the cross in a way that shows both His justice and His mercy together, Romans 3:26. The church is still warned from the wilderness history, 1 Corinthians 10:11, because the final gathering has not yet come, but the warnings are given to a people who already stand in the breach-filling work of Christ.

The new creation is where the psalm's last prayer is finally answered. In Revelation 7:9 a great multitude from every nation, tribe, people and language stands before the throne, and the song of the redeemed is not a confession of failure but a cry of salvation, Revelation 7:10. The land that was polluted with blood is replaced by a city where nothing unclean enters, Revelation 21:27, and the God who is praised from everlasting to everlasting now dwells with His people, Revelation 21:3. The people of verse 48 who say 'Amen' find in the end that the Amen has been spoken for them.

sermon.title: A Pastor's Role in World Missions
sermon.why: Piper anchors this message in Psalm 106:7-8, Yet He saved them for the sake of His name, to make His power known, tracing that same principle, God acting for His own glory rather than human worthiness, through the whole sweep of redemptive history; it directly illuminates this psalm's central turn, that mercy triumphed over Israel's rebellion because of God's name, not their merit.

quiz.q: According to verses 7-8, why did God save Israel at the Red Sea despite their rebellion there?

options.text: For the sake of His own name, to make His power known.
options.note: The psalm is explicit that God's motive was His own name and power, not Israel's worthiness, since they had just rebelled.

options.text: Because Israel had repented thoroughly before crossing the sea.
options.note: The text says they rebelled at the sea; the rescue is attributed to God's name, not prior repentance.

options.text: Because Moses bribed God with a sacrifice.
options.note: No such bribery is described; the psalm credits God's own name and power as the reason for salvation.

options.text: Because the Egyptians surrendered without a fight.
options.note: The Egyptians pursued and were destroyed in the sea, verse 11; they did not surrender.

quiz.q: What did Israel do at Horeb, according to verses 19-20?

options.text: They made a calf and worshiped a molten image, exchanging their Glory for the image of a grass-eating ox.
options.note: The golden calf incident, Exodus 32, is the clearest instance in the psalm of Israel trading the living God for a lifeless idol.

options.text: They built the tabernacle exactly as God commanded.
options.note: The tabernacle's faithful construction is not in view here; this passage describes the golden calf, an act of rebellion, not obedience.

options.text: They fasted and prayed for forty days.
options.note: Moses fasted on the mountain, but the people below were making and worshiping the calf, the opposite of faithful prayer.

options.text: They asked Aaron to intercede for their sins.
options.note: Aaron in fact made the calf for them; it was Moses, not a request through Aaron, who later interceded, verse 23.

quiz.q: Who stood in the breach to turn away God's wrath after the golden calf, verse 23?

options.text: Moses, God's chosen one.
options.note: Moses' intercession, recorded fully in Exodus 32:11-14, prevented God's decreed destruction of the people.

options.text: Aaron, the high priest.
options.note: Aaron had made the calf; it was Moses who interceded to turn away God's wrath.

options.text: Phinehas, the priest.
options.note: Phinehas' zeal comes later in the psalm, at Baal of Peor, verses 28-31, not at the golden calf.

options.text: Joshua, Moses' assistant.
options.note: The text specifically names Moses as the one who stood in the breach, not Joshua.

quiz.q: What does the psalm say happened when Phinehas intervened at Baal of Peor, verses 30-31?

options.text: The plague was restrained, and it was credited to him as righteousness for endless generations.
options.note: This directly echoes the language of Genesis 15:6, righteousness credited by faith, applied here to Phinehas' zealous act.

options.text: The plague grew worse and spread to neighboring nations.
options.note: The text says the plague was restrained by his intervention, not that it worsened.

options.text: He was punished for taking matters into his own hands.
options.note: The text credits his action as righteousness, the opposite of punishment.

options.text: He was made king over Israel as a reward.
options.note: The reward named in the text is that his act was credited as righteousness, not a royal appointment.

quiz.q: What is the psalm's closing plea, verse 47?

options.text: Save us, O LORD our God, and gather us from the nations, that we may give thanks to Your holy name.
options.note: The confession of repeated failure ends not in despair but in a plea for salvation and gathering, resting on God's character rather than Israel's record.

options.text: Give us a king who will never sin.
options.note: No such request appears; the plea is for God's salvation and gathering, not for a sinless human king.

options.text: Let us remain scattered so we may learn humility.
options.note: The plea is the opposite, to be gathered from the nations, not to remain scattered.

options.text: Grant us victory over all our earthly enemies.
options.note: The specific request named is salvation and gathering for the purpose of praise, not simply military victory.

questions: The psalm opens with the confession, we have sinned like our fathers, verse 6. What patterns of sin do you see repeating in your own life that echo failures you have seen in others before you?
Verse 13 says Israel soon forgot His works after the Red Sea. What recent evidence of God's faithfulness in your life are you already at risk of forgetting?

God saved Israel for the sake of His own name, verse 8, not because they deserved it. How does resting your assurance on God's character rather than your own performance change the way you pray today?

Moses stood in the breach to turn away wrath, verse 23, a picture fulfilled in Christ's ongoing intercession for us, Hebrews 7:25. How does knowing Christ is praying for you right now change how you face your own failure?

The psalm ends with a plea to be gathered and to give thanks, verse 47, even after cataloging so much failure. What would it look like for you to move from shame over past sin to an honest plea for God's ongoing mercy?

Reflect on the whole sweep of this psalm: God rescues, Israel forgets, God rescues again. Where in your life do you need to trust that God's steadfast love, not your consistency, is what holds your relationship with Him together?

translationNotes.note: The Red Sea can also be rendered the Sea of Reeds, reflecting uncertainty about the precise body of water; the same alternate rendering applies in verses 9 and 22.
Their Glory, referring to God Himself, can also be rendered their glorious God; either way the verse describes the tragedy of exchanging the living God for a lifeless image.
Meribah means quarreling in Hebrew, naming the place after Israel's conflict with God there, compare Exodus 17:7.
